title: ser vs estar
tagline: Both mean 'to be' — but ser is identity, estar is state. The rule about permanent vs temporary will get you in trouble.

sides.core: Ser encodes what something fundamentally is — identity, category, origin, material.

examples.note: His personality. Swap to está and he's just bored right now — totally different verdict.

examples.es: La boda es en la iglesia.
examples.en: The wedding is at the church.
examples.note: Location of an event uses ser, not estar. Catches everyone out.
Appearance as identity. But 'está muy guapa hoy' means she looks great today — she made an effort.

sides.core: Estar encodes current state — how something is right now, not what it is.

examples.note: Death is permanent but it's still a state the body is in. 'Es muerto' doesn't exist.
Quality you're experiencing right now. 'Es bueno' is a general verdict; 'está bueno' is tasting it.
Versus 'es listo' = he's clever. Same adjective, completely different meaning depending on verb.

tricky: Adjectives that flip meaning: listo (clever/ready), malo (bad/sick), bueno (good/tasty), vivo (sharp/alive), seguro (safe/certain).

title: fue vs era
tagline: Both are past tense of ser — fue is a completed snapshot, era is the background scenery.

sides.core: Preterite — the event happened, it's done, you're delivering a verdict on it.

examples.note: The night is over. You're wrapping it up. Preterite = closing the bracket.
That friendship has ended — he moved away, you fell out, or he died. Fue signals it's finished.
Asking for an overall verdict on a completed event.

sides.core: Imperfect — ongoing background state, what was true across a whole period.

examples.es: Cuando era niño, era muy tímido.
examples.en: When I was a child, I was very shy.
examples.note: No specific moment — a quality that lasted across years of childhood.

examples.es: Era un día tranquilo cuando llegó la noticia.
examples.en: It was a quiet day when the news arrived.
examples.note: Era sets the atmosphere; llegó (preterite) is the event that cut through it.
Just remembering a time — no implication the friendship ended badly. Compare fue mi amigo.

tricky: 'Fue' vs 'era' with the same sentence changes meaning: 'fue mi amigo' (friendship ended) vs 'era mi amigo' (fond memory of a time). Native speakers feel this immediately.

title: por vs para
tagline: Para points forward to a goal or recipient. Por looks back at cause, exchange, or movement through.

sides.core: Destination, purpose, recipient, deadline, or a surprising contrast given the subject.

examples.en: I did it for you (you'll benefit).
examples.note: The action is aimed at you as its destination. Compare: 'lo hice por ti' = because of you / for your sake.

examples.es: Para ser extranjero, hablas muy bien.
examples.en: For a foreigner, you speak really well.
examples.note: Sets up a contrast — given what you are, this is unexpected. A sideways compliment.
Monday is the deadline — the destination in time. Por lunes would mean 'around Monday.'

sides.core: Cause, exchange, duration, movement through space, or on behalf of.

examples.en: I did it because of you / for your sake.
examples.note: You're the reason, not the recipient. The motivation, not the destination.
Movement through or along. Para la playa would mean you were heading to the beach as a destination.

examples.en: I was ill for a week.
examples.note: Duration. How long the state lasted. Para una semana would imply a deadline.

tricky: 'Gracias por todo' uses por (exchange — you're acknowledging what they gave). Never 'gracias para.' And 'por' in passive voice: 'fue escrito por Cervantes' = written by Cervantes.

title: saber vs conocer
tagline: Saber is knowing facts and skills. Conocer is familiarity through experience — people, places, things you've encountered.

sides.core: Knowing information, knowing how to do something, or knowing a fact.

examples.en: I know how to speak Spanish.
examples.note: Ability or skill always uses saber. 'Conozco hablar' simply doesn't work.

examples.en: Do you know where the pharmacy is?
examples.note: A piece of information — its location. Conocer would mean you've personally visited it.

examples.en: I don't know what to tell you.
examples.note: Knowing what to say = information/ability. Natural and very common.

sides.core: Personal familiarity — you've been there, met them, experienced it firsthand.

examples.note: You've lived there, walked its streets. Not information about Madrid — the city itself through experience.

examples.en: Have you come across this book?
examples.note: You can 'conocer' a book — it means you've encountered it. Not the same as knowing its contents (saber).

examples.en: I don't know her in person.
examples.note: Meeting someone personally = conocer. 'Sé quién es' means I know who she is — just information.

tricky: 'Sé que es famoso' (I know he's famous — a fact) vs 'lo conozco' (I know him — we've met). The distinction maps cleanly to French savoir/connaître or German wissen/kennen.

title: salir vs quedar
tagline: Quedar is making the plan to meet. Salir is the activity of going out. You can have one without the other.

sides.core: Going out — leaving the house, doing an activity, or dating someone.

examples.en: I went out with my friends last night.
examples.note: The activity — you went somewhere together. The evening happened.

examples.en: Are you seeing someone? / Are you dating anyone?
examples.note: 'Salir con alguien' also means to date. Context usually makes it clear, but worth knowing.

examples.es: No me apetece salir esta noche.
examples.en: I don't feel like going out tonight.
examples.note: Salir = leaving the house. Quedar could still happen at home.

sides.core: Arranging to meet — the plan, the agreement, the arrangement. Common in Spain.

examples.en: Shall we meet up Friday? / Are we on for Friday?
examples.note: The arrangement itself. You could then go anywhere. Quedar is the plan, not the outing.

examples.es: Quedé con ella pero al final no salimos.
examples.en: We arranged to meet but we didn't end up going out.
examples.note: Quedar (plan) without salir (activity). They're two separate things.

examples.es: Quedamos en el bar de siempre.
examples.en: We arranged to meet at the usual bar.
examples.note: Quedar + en = where you're meeting. Very natural, very common in Spain.

tricky: In Latin America, 'quedar' for arranging to meet is less common — they'd say 'juntarse' or 'encontrarse.' If you're in Mexico saying '¿quedamos?' people might look confused.

title: llevar vs hacer (time)
tagline: Both express how long something has been going on — but they're built differently and can't be swapped.

sides.core: How long you've been doing something continuously — built into the verb itself.

examples.en: I've been living here for three years.
examples.note: Llevar + time + gerund. The ongoing action is baked in. Elegant and very Spanish.

examples.en: I'd been waiting for two hours.
examples.note: Imperfect of llevar for past ongoing. Works exactly the same way.

examples.en: How long have you been learning Spanish?
examples.note: The natural way to ask. 'Hace cuánto' also works but this sounds more fluent.

sides.core: Hace + time + que — how long ago something started, or how long since something happened.

examples.es: Hace tres años que vivo aquí.
examples.en: I've been living here for three years.
examples.note: Same meaning as the llevar version but different structure. Both are correct; llevar feels more natural in speech.

examples.es: Hace dos horas que te espero.
examples.en: I've been waiting for you for two hours.
examples.note: Emphasis on duration from the speaker's point of view. Slightly more dramatic than llevar.

examples.es: Hacía mucho que no te veía.
examples.en: It had been a long time since I'd seen you.
examples.note: Imperfect hacer for past context. Common opener after a long absence.

tricky: English speakers often try 'estoy viviendo aquí por tres años' — wrong on two counts. Spanish doesn't use present continuous for ongoing duration, and por isn't used this way. Use llevar or hace.

title: pedir vs preguntar
tagline: Preguntar is asking a question. Pedir is asking for something — a request, an order, a demand.

sides.core: To request, to order, to ask for something — you want something from someone.

examples.note: Ordering food and drink is always pedir. Never preguntar.

examples.en: I'm asking you to listen to me.
examples.note: Pedir + que + subjunctive for making requests of people.
'Pedir perdón' = to apologise. A fixed phrase — you're requesting forgiveness.

sides.core: To ask a question — you want information, not a thing.

examples.en: She asked me what my name was.
examples.note: Seeking information. Preguntar + indirect question.

examples.es: Pregúntale a él, yo no sé.
examples.note: Directing someone to ask elsewhere. Always preguntar for questions.
Preguntarse = to wonder. A reflexive use that English speakers often miss.

tricky: 'Ask him for the bill' = 'pídele la cuenta' (request). 'Ask him what time it is' = 'pregúntale qué hora es' (question). The English verb 'ask' covers both — Spanish doesn't.

title: poder vs saber (can)
tagline: Both translate as 'can' — but poder is physical ability or permission, saber is knowing how.

sides.core: Can in the sense of being able to, being allowed to, or it being possible.

examples.note: Circumstantial — you're busy, unwell, not permitted. Not about skill.

examples.en: Can you smoke here? / Is smoking allowed?
examples.note: Impersonal poder for permission. Very natural way to ask if something is allowed.
One of the most useful phrases in Spanish. Possibility, not ability.

sides.core: Can in the sense of knowing how — a skill you've learned.

examples.note: You never learned. Poder here would mean you're physically prevented from swimming right now.

examples.en: Can you drive? / Do you know how to drive?
examples.note: Skill. Poder conduces would mean 'are you allowed to drive' or 'are you in a state to drive.'

examples.es: De pequeña sabía tocar el piano.
examples.en: When she was little she could play piano.
examples.note: Past ability/skill. Podía here would imply she was allowed or physically capable — different meaning.

tricky: '¿Puedes tocar el piano?' = Are you able to right now / are you allowed to? '¿Sabes tocar el piano?' = Do you know how? The question you mean to ask is almost always saber.

title: deber vs tener que
tagline: Both mean 'must' or 'have to' — deber is moral obligation, tener que is practical necessity.

sides.core: Moral duty, obligation you owe — what you should do as a matter of principle.

examples.note: Moral imperative. Tener que ser honesto would sound more like a practical requirement.
Conditional of deber = should. The most natural way to express mild obligation in Spanish.

examples.en: I must be right. / I'm probably right.
examples.note: 'Deber de' (with de) = probability, not obligation. 'Debo tener razón' = I have a duty to be right. Huge difference.

sides.core: Practical necessity — you have to do it because of circumstances.

examples.es: Tengo que irme, el tren sale en diez minutos.
examples.en: I have to go, the train leaves in ten minutes.
examples.note: External circumstance forcing the action. No moral dimension — just logistics.

examples.en: You have to try this wine.
examples.note: Strong recommendation. Tener que is common for this in everyday speech.
Circumstances left no choice. Debí mentir would sound like you had a duty to lie — odd.

tricky: 'Deber de + infinitive' (deduction: 'must be') vs 'deber + infinitive' (obligation: 'must do'). The tiny 'de' changes everything. 'Debe de estar cansado' = he must be tired. 'Debe estar aquí' = he's supposed to be here.

title: ir vs venir
tagline: Spanish anchors movement to where the speaker is right now — the opposite of English more often than you'd think.

sides.core: To go — movement away from the current location of the speaker.

examples.note: Speaker is leaving from where they are. Standard use.
Spanish says 'I'm going' even when English says 'coming.' Because you're moving away from where you currently are toward them.

examples.es: Fueron a Barcelona el verano pasado.
examples.en: They went to Barcelona last summer.
examples.note: Movement to somewhere away from the reference point — even in the past.

sides.core: To come — movement toward the speaker's current location.

examples.en: Are you coming to the party?
examples.note: The speaker is at (or going to) the party. They're inviting you to join where they'll be.
Movement toward the speaker. The most basic use.
Venir de = coming from somewhere. The movement ends at the speaker's current position.

tricky: On the phone: '¿Puedes venir?' (Can you come here — to where I am?) vs '¿Puedo ir?' (Can I come — to where you are?). English uses 'come' for both. Spanish tracks the speaker's anchor point.

title: traer vs llevar
tagline: Like ir/venir but for objects — llevar is taking something away, traer is bringing it here.

sides.core: To take/carry — moving something away from the speaker's current position.

examples.es: Lleva el paraguas, que va a llover.
examples.en: Take an umbrella, it's going to rain.
examples.note: You're sending them off with it. They're leaving your location.
Even though English says 'bring,' the waiter is moving away from their current spot to deliver it — so Spanish uses llevar.

examples.en: How long have you been waiting?
examples.note: A completely different meaning of llevar — time elapsed. Context makes it clear.

sides.core: To bring — moving something toward the speaker's current position.

examples.en: Can you get me a beer?
examples.note: You're asking them to bring it to where you are. The destination is your location.

examples.en: I brought wine to the dinner.
examples.note: Brought it to the location you're describing — the dinner, where you were going.
Traer used figuratively — bringing information to the speaker.

tricky: 'El camarero trae la cuenta' (waiter brings the bill — to the customer's table, where the speaker is). But 'llévame a casa' (take me home — away from current location). The anchor is always the speaker.

title: querer vs amar
tagline: Both mean 'to love' — but querer is the everyday word for love and wanting, amar is deeper and more formal.

sides.core: To love (people, pets) and to want (things). The everyday word for both.

examples.note: The standard way to tell someone you love them — partner, family, close friends. Natural and warm.
Wanting things. The same verb. Context makes love vs desire obvious.

examples.en: Do you want us to come?
examples.note: Querer + que + subjunctive for wanting someone else to do something.

sides.core: Deeper, more elevated love — romantic, profound, or poetic. Less used in daily speech.

examples.note: More intense than te quiero. In Spain, te quiero is more common; in Latin America, te amo is more used in romantic contexts.
Deep passion for something. More literary than 'le gusta mucho' or 'le encanta.'
Religious/formal register. Amar carries weight that querer doesn't always have.

tricky: In Spain, 'te amo' can sound overly dramatic in a relationship — 'te quiero' is the natural thing to say to a partner. In Mexico and much of Latin America, 'te amo' is the go-to for romantic love. Know your region.

title: mirar vs ver
tagline: Mirar is looking (actively directing your gaze). Ver is seeing (the result — what registers in your eyes).

sides.core: To look at — you're directing your attention intentionally.

examples.note: An active choice to direct your gaze. You're telling someone to look.

examples.en: Don't look at me like that.
examples.note: The gaze is intentional and directed. Mirar = the act of looking.
Active, deliberate attention. Ver menú would mean they can see it — different thing.

sides.core: To see — what your eyes register, or watching something over time (TV, film).

examples.note: Not asking if they looked — asking if the keys entered their field of vision.
Watching TV uses ver, not mirar. Fixed phrase — don't swap them.

examples.es: Desde aquí no se ve nada.
examples.en: You can't see anything from here.
examples.note: Visibility — what the eyes can register from a position. Nothing active about it.

tricky: ¡Mira! = Look! (directing attention). ¿Ves? = Do you see? / You see what I mean? (comprehension or visibility). In conversation, '¿ves?' is constantly used to check understanding — like 'you know?' in English.

title: escuchar vs oír
tagline: Escuchar is listening (active). Oír is hearing (passive — sound entering your ears whether you want it or not).

sides.core: To listen — you're paying attention, you chose to engage with the sound.

examples.note: Command to pay attention. Active, intentional.

examples.es: Me encanta escuchar música por las mañanas.
examples.en: I love listening to music in the mornings.
examples.note: Deliberate, enjoyable listening.
The complaint isn't about hearing — it's about attention and engagement.

sides.core: To hear — the sound reaches your ears, with or without your intention.

examples.en: Do you hear that? What's that noise?
examples.note: Something that just entered your auditory field — you didn't seek it out.

examples.es: Se oían voces desde la calle.
examples.en: Voices could be heard from the street.
examples.note: Passive hearing — sounds coming in from outside. Se oír is very natural for this.
'Oye' as a conversational opener = 'hey' or 'listen.' One of the most common words in spoken Spanish.

tricky: 'Oye' (from oír) is used constantly as a filler — 'Oye, ¿qué haces este finde?' It doesn't literally mean 'hear.' But escucha as a conversation opener sounds more formal and urgent.

title: acordarse vs recordar
tagline: Both mean 'to remember' — acordarse is reflexive and personal, recordar can also mean to remind.

sides.core: To remember (reflexive) — the memory comes to you, often as a task or something important.

examples.en: Did you remember to call him?
examples.note: Remembering to do something. Acordarse de + infinitive is very common for this.

examples.es: No me acuerdo de su nombre.
examples.note: The name isn't coming to you. Reflexive construction — the forgetting is happening to you.

examples.es: Me acuerdo de cuando éramos jóvenes.
examples.en: I remember when we were young.
examples.note: Nostalgic recall. Acordarse de + noun/clause.

sides.core: To remember OR to remind someone — can be transitive with a direct object.

examples.note: Direct object — the memory is a thing you hold. More deliberate than acordarse.

examples.en: Remind me to call the doctor.
examples.note: Recordar = to remind. Acordarme can't do this. Key difference.

examples.en: It reminds me of my grandmother.
examples.note: Recordar a = to remind someone of something. Very useful, often missed.

tricky: 'Recuérdame' = remind me (you tell someone else to prompt you). 'Recuérdalo tú' = you remember it / remind him. Acordarse can't function as 'remind' — only recordar has that power.

title: sentir vs sentirse
tagline: Sentir is feeling or sensing something external. Sentirse is how you feel inside — your personal emotional state.

sides.core: To feel or sense something — an external thing, a sensation, or to feel sorry about something.

examples.note: A physical sensation you're registering. Not your inner state — the cold is external.
'Lo siento' = I'm sorry. Fixed phrase. Sentirse lo would be wrong.
An intuition or feeling about something outside yourself.

sides.core: To feel (reflexive) — your internal emotional or physical state.

examples.note: Your internal state — how you are. Siento fatal would mean you sense something terrible.
Emotional state — it belongs to her inner world.
The standard way to ask about someone's wellbeing. ¿Cómo sientes? would be asking what they're sensing — odd.

tricky: 'Siento frío' (I feel cold — external sensation) vs 'me siento bien' (I feel well — internal state). The reflexive signals the feeling is about yourself. Mix them up and you change what the feeling is about.

title: pensar vs creer
tagline: Both translate as 'to think' — pensar is active thinking or planning, creer is holding a belief.

sides.core: To think actively — reasoning, planning, having opinions about something.

examples.en: What do you think about this?
examples.note: Asking for an opinion or reaction. Pensar en = thinking about; pensar de = thinking of (opinion).

examples.en: I'm thinking of going tomorrow. / I plan to go.
examples.note: Pensar + infinitive = to plan or intend. Very common. Not creer.
Active mental occupation. Pensar en = to think about (someone/something).

sides.core: To believe, to think in the sense of holding a view or assumption.

examples.note: Expressing a belief or opinion. The most natural 'I think' in conversation.

examples.es: No creo que sea buena idea.
examples.en: I don't think it's a good idea.
examples.note: Negated creer triggers subjunctive. One of the most reliable subjunctive triggers.
Conversational skepticism or interest. Extremely common filler response.

tricky: 'Pienso que' and 'creo que' both work for opinions, but 'pienso que no' (I don't think so) is less common than 'creo que no.' And 'pienso en ir' (I'm considering going) vs 'creo que iré' (I think I'll go) — subtle but real.

title: gastar vs pasar (spend)
tagline: Both translate 'to spend' in English — gastar is spending money, pasar is spending time.

sides.core: To spend money, or to use up / waste something.

examples.es: Gastó todo el sueldo en ropa.
examples.en: She spent her whole salary on clothes.
examples.note: Money being spent. Pasar el sueldo would mean 'pass the salary' — nonsense.
Gastar = to use up a resource. Wider than just money.
The natural question about expenditure.

sides.core: To spend time, to happen, to pass — one of the most versatile verbs in Spanish.

examples.en: We spent the summer in Galicia.
examples.note: Time, not money. Gastamos el verano would be wrong.
To happen — one of pasar's most common uses. Completely different from spending.
Pasarlo bien/mal = to have a good/bad time. Fixed idiom.

tricky: English 'spend' covers both. Spanish splits them cleanly. The error 'gasté tres horas esperando' (I spent three hours waiting) sounds like you paid for the waiting. Use 'pasé tres horas esperando' or 'estuve tres horas esperando.'

title: hablar vs decir
tagline: Hablar is talking (the activity). Decir is saying or telling (the content of what's communicated).

sides.core: To speak or talk — the act of using language, not the content.

examples.note: The activity of talking — not what he says.
Ability to use a language. Always hablar. Never decir español.

examples.en: We need to talk about this.
examples.note: Hablar de = to talk about something. The conversation itself.

sides.core: To say or tell — focusing on the content, the words, the message.

examples.en: What are you saying? / What do you mean?
examples.note: The content of speech. Also used as 'what?' when you didn't catch something.
Decir = to tell. Very common. Hablé would mean I spoke — not that I conveyed a specific thing.

examples.en: That is to say... / In other words...
examples.note: Fixed phrase — one of the most useful discourse markers in Spanish.

tricky: 'Dime' = tell me (the content). 'Háblame' = talk to me (the act, the connection). 'Me dijo que vendría' = he told me he'd come (content). 'Habló conmigo' = he talked with me (the conversation happened).'

title: encontrar vs buscar
tagline: Buscar is the searching. Encontrar is the finding. One is the journey, one is the result.

sides.core: To look for, to search — the process of seeking. Crucially: no 'for' needed in Spanish.

examples.note: No 'por' or 'para' needed. Buscar already means 'look for' — buscar por is wrong.

examples.en: He's been looking for work for months.
examples.note: The search is ongoing. He hasn't found it yet.

examples.en: Can you look up a flight for me?
examples.note: Search in the digital sense too. Completely natural.

sides.core: To find, or to find (in the sense of consider/think) — the discovery.

examples.note: The search (buscar) ended. This is the result.

examples.en: I find this book really interesting.
examples.note: Encontrar = to find in the opinion sense. Very common. Like French 'trouver.'

examples.en: We ran into each other by chance.
examples.note: Encontrarse = to meet/run into someone. Reflexive use.

tricky: English speakers say 'buscar por' because 'look for' has 'for.' Spanish doesn't need it. And 'encontrar' for opinions ('lo encuentro aburrido') is something many learners miss — they use 'pensar' instead, which also works but is less idiomatic.

title: perder vs faltar
tagline: Perder is losing something. Faltar is something being missing or absent — the gap itself.

sides.core: To lose — an active experience where something slips from your possession or control.

examples.note: You had it and now you don't. The losing is something that happened to you.
To lose a game or competition. Always perder.
Perder el tiempo = to waste time. Fixed idiom.

sides.core: To be missing, to lack, to be absent — it works like gustar (the missing thing is the subject).

examples.note: The euros are what's missing — they're the subject. Me = indirect object. Like gustar.

examples.en: María is missing / María hasn't shown up.
examples.note: María is absent. Nothing was lost — she just isn't there.

examples.en: We're nearly there. / Not far now.
examples.note: Time or distance remaining. Very common in travel contexts.

tricky: 'Me falta práctica' = I lack practice (it's missing from my life). 'Perdí la práctica' = I lost the skill I once had. One is about absence, one is about losing something you possessed. Different feelings entirely.

title: tocar vs jugar
tagline: Both can relate to playing — jugar is playing games/sports, tocar is playing instruments and also 'touching.'

sides.core: To touch, and to play an instrument — plus several idiomatic meanings around turns and luck.

examples.es: Toca la guitarra desde los doce años.
examples.en: She's been playing guitar since she was twelve.
examples.note: Instruments always use tocar. Jugar la guitarra is wrong.
Tocar = to be someone's turn. Completely different from playing or touching.
Tocar for luck — something coming to you. 'Me tocó' is how you describe a windfall.

sides.core: To play games, sports, or to gamble — activities with rules and outcomes.

examples.es: Juegan al fútbol todos los domingos.
examples.note: Sports and games use jugar. Note: jugar al in Spain, jugar fútbol in Latin America.

examples.es: De niño jugaba mucho con Lego.
examples.en: As a child I played a lot with Lego.
examples.note: Play as a child's activity — jugar.
Figurative: taking dangerous risks. Idiomatic use of jugar.

tricky: '¿A qué juegas?' = What game are you playing? '¿Qué tocas?' = What instrument do you play? Confuse them and you get: 'toco al fútbol' (I touch the football — odd) or 'juego la guitarra' (wrong). The rule is strict.

title: volver vs regresar
tagline: Both mean 'to return' — volver is universal Spanish, regresar is more Latin American and slightly more formal.

sides.core: To return, to come back — the standard word in Spain and widely used everywhere.

examples.note: One of the most useful phrases. Regresar would work but sounds slightly stiff here.

examples.es: Volver a + infinitivo = to do something again.
examples.en: Volvió a llamar = He called again.
examples.note: Volver a + infinitive is how Spanish says 'again.' Extremely useful structure.
Natural in all registers. The default return verb in Spain.

sides.core: To return/go back — preferred in much of Latin America, more formal in Spain.

examples.es: Regresaron al pueblo de sus padres.
examples.en: They returned to their parents' village.
examples.note: Sounds slightly more formal or literary than volvieron. Both correct.
Common in Mexico and much of Latin America where regresar is the natural word.
Vuelta (noun from volver) in an idiom — regresar doesn't have this idiomatic reach.

tricky: Volver has far more idiomatic reach: 'volver en sí' (to come to/regain consciousness), 'volver loco' (to drive mad), 'volver a ver' (to see again). Regresar can't do any of these. Learn volver first.

title: dejar vs salir (leave)
tagline: English 'leave' covers both — dejar is leaving something/someone behind, salir is leaving a place.

sides.core: To leave something/someone — you're parting from a person or object, or letting something happen.

examples.note: Leaving a person — ending a relationship. Salir de would mean she physically left him (walked away).

examples.es: Deja el abrigo en la silla.
examples.en: Leave the coat on the chair.
examples.note: Leaving an object somewhere. Never salir for this.
Dejar = to let, to leave someone in a state. 'Sal de aquí' would be 'get out of here' — different.

sides.core: To leave a place — physical departure from a location.

examples.es: Sale del trabajo a las seis.
examples.note: Leaving a place. Always salir for departures from locations.

examples.es: El tren sale a las ocho.
examples.note: Departure of transport — always salir.

examples.en: He ran out / He left running.
examples.note: Salir + gerund for how someone left. Vivid and common.

tricky: 'Dejé el trabajo' = I quit the job (left it behind as a thing). 'Salí del trabajo' = I left the office (physical departure). In English both are 'I left work' — Spanish forces you to decide what you mean.

title: ser vs parecer
tagline: Ser states what something is. Parecer hedges — it seems, it looks like, you have an impression.

sides.core: States a fact about identity or essence — you're committing to this being true.

examples.note: A direct verdict. You're declaring it interesting.
Character as fact. Parecer would soften this to an impression.
Identity, category — what you are to each other.

sides.core: To seem, to appear, to look like — your impression, not a definite fact.

examples.note: You're reading the signs, not making a diagnosis. Much softer than 'está cansado.'

examples.en: What do you think? / How does it seem to you?
examples.note: Asking for an opinion or reaction. One of the most useful phrases in Spanish.

examples.en: It looks like it's going to rain.
examples.note: Impression from evidence — dark clouds, humidity. Not a forecast fact.

tricky: 'Me parece bien' = I think that's fine / it seems good to me. This is not the same as 'es bueno' (it is good). Parecer adds a layer of subjectivity. Very useful for being politely non-committal in Spanish.

title: haber
tagline: The invisible backbone of Spanish — auxiliary 'have' for perfect tenses AND the existence word 'hay'. Two completely different jobs, one verb.

sides.core: As 'hay' it means 'there is/are' — existence. It never changes for singular vs plural, which catches everyone out.

examples.es: Hay un problema. / Hay muchos problemas.
examples.en: There is a problem. / There are many problems.
examples.note: Same word for singular and plural. 'Hay muchos' not 'han muchos.' Never agrees with the noun.
Hay for existence in questions. 'Está algo de comer' would mean the food is located somewhere — different.

examples.en: There were a lot of people.
examples.note: Imperfect of haber for past existence. Again — singular form for plural noun. No exceptions.

sides.core: Forms all perfect tenses — he comido, había llegado, habrá salido. Never replaced by tener in this role.

examples.note: Perfect tense — haber + past participle. Never 'tengo comido' in standard Spanish (it exists in some regions but avoid it).

examples.es: Si hubiera sabido, no habría venido.
examples.en: If I had known, I wouldn't have come.
examples.note: Pluperfect subjunctive + conditional perfect. Both built from haber. Essential for hypotheticals.
Haber used in an infinitive clause after modal. 'Debe de haber' — not 'debe de hay.'

tricky: 'Hay' never changes: 'hay un libro' AND 'hay veinte libros.' This violates learners' instinct. And never confuse hay (existence) with está (location): 'hay una farmacia por aquí' (there's a pharmacy around here) vs 'la farmacia está en la esquina' (the pharmacy is on the corner).

title: tener
tagline: Tener means 'to have' — but Spanish uses it where English says 'to be', making a whole class of sentences feel backwards.

sides.core: Possession — physical, abstract, and relational. Standard 'to have.'

examples.note: Straightforward possession. No surprises here.

examples.en: She has a lot of talent.
examples.note: Abstract possession. Also normal.
Tener que + infinitive = have to. The workhorse of obligation in Spanish.

sides.core: Used where English says 'to be' — for age, hunger, thirst, heat, cold, fear, luck, and more. These must be memorised.

examples.es: Tengo hambre / sed / frío / calor / sueño / miedo.
examples.en: I'm hungry / thirsty / cold / hot / sleepy / scared.
examples.note: All of these use tener in Spanish, not ser or estar. 'Estoy hambriento' exists but is less common; 'soy hambre' is wrong.
Age uses tener, not ser. 'Tengo treinta años' = I am thirty. Never 'soy treinta años.'
'Tener razón' = to be right. Fixed phrase. 'Estás correcto' works too but 'tener razón' is more natural.

tricky: The tener expressions (hambre, sed, miedo, razón, suerte, prisa) are non-negotiable fixed phrases. Don't try to logic your way to them — just learn the list. 'Estoy con hambre' is heard in some regions but 'tengo hambre' is universal.

title: hacer
tagline: Hacer means make and do — but it also does weather, time expressions, and causatives. One of the most overloaded verbs in Spanish.

sides.core: The default verb for doing and making — covers both where English uses two different words.

examples.es: Haz los deberes. / Haz la cama.
examples.en: Do your homework. / Make the bed.
examples.note: Both 'do' and 'make' use hacer. Spanish doesn't distinguish — context handles it.
General doing. The verb of effort and action.

examples.en: What are you doing? / What do you do?
examples.note: Both the present action and profession can be asked this way. Context (or tense) clarifies.

sides.core: Weather and time elapsed both use hacer — with no subject pronoun, and always singular.

examples.note: Weather uses hacer impersonally. Never 'está frío' for the weather (that's for objects being cold to touch).

examples.es: Hace tres años que vivo aquí.
examples.en: I've been living here for three years.
examples.note: Hace + time + que = how long something has been happening. Present tense for ongoing situations.

examples.es: Hacía mucho que no te veía.
examples.en: It had been a long time since I'd seen you.
examples.note: Imperfect hacer for past elapsed time. Common opener after a gap.

tricky: 'Hace' for weather is impersonal — never 'él hace frío.' And 'hacer' as a causative: 'Me hizo reír' (he made me laugh), 'Lo hizo llorar' (it made him cry). The causative hacer + infinitive is a structure English learners consistently miss.

title: dar
tagline: Dar means 'to give' — but it powers dozens of expressions where English uses completely different verbs.

sides.core: Physical and abstract giving — standard use.

examples.note: Direct request. The imperative dame is extremely common.
Dar las gracias = to thank. Not a giving of thanks — just the phrase for it.

examples.en: To go for a walk / a stroll.
examples.note: Dar + noun creates action phrases. You're not giving a walk — you're taking one.

sides.core: Dar powers fear, opinions, feelings, and reactions — where English uses completely different verbs.

examples.en: It scares me / I'm scared of it.
examples.note: Dar miedo = to scare. The fear comes to you — reverse structure like gustar.

examples.en: It's all the same to me. / I don't mind.
examples.note: One of the most useful phrases in Spanish. Dar igual = to not matter, to be indifferent.
Shame/embarrassment arrives at you via dar. 'Estoy avergonzado' also works but dar vergüenza is more common.

tricky: The dar expressions all follow the gustar structure — the thing causing the reaction is the subject: 'las alturas me dan miedo' (heights scare me). Learners say 'yo doy miedo a las alturas' — backwards. Also: 'dar con' = to find/come across: '¡Di con la solución!' = I hit on the solution.

title: poner
tagline: Poner is 'to put' — but it also sets tables, turns things on, gives names, and becomes ponerse for a whole world of change-of-state expressions.

sides.core: Physical placing and abstract putting — and turning on devices.

examples.note: Poner la mesa = to set the table. Not placing the table — a fixed phrase.

examples.en: Put the TV on / put some music on.
examples.note: Turning on appliances uses poner, not encender in everyday speech — though both work.
Poner = to say/read (on a sign, label, screen). Surprisingly common.

sides.core: Reflexive ponerse = to put on (clothing) OR to become (a change of state).

examples.note: Wearing clothes: ponerse for the action of putting on. Llevar for the state of wearing.
Ponerse + adjective = to become (involuntary physical or emotional change). Se puso triste, furioso, nervioso.

examples.es: Se pone muy pesado cuando bebe.
examples.en: He gets really annoying when he drinks.
examples.note: Ponerse for becoming a quality — temporary, change-of-state. Not ser (identity) or estar (current state).

tricky: Ponerse vs volverse vs hacerse vs quedarse — all mean 'to become' but for different types of change. Ponerse = involuntary emotional/physical change. Volverse = deeper personality change. Hacerse = deliberate transformation. Quedarse = ending up in a state. This quartet is genuinely one of the hardest things in Spanish.

title: gustar
tagline: Gustar doesn't mean 'to like' — it means 'to please.' The thing you like is the subject. The sentence runs in reverse.

sides.core: The thing liked is the grammatical subject. Me gusta = it pleases me. Me gustan = they please me.

examples.es: Me gusta el café. / Me gustan los gatos.
examples.en: I like coffee. / I like cats.
examples.note: Singular coffee → gusta. Plural cats → gustan. The verb agrees with the thing liked, not the person.
Infinitive as subject = always singular. '¿Te gustan vivir?' is wrong even though there might be many aspects of living here.

examples.es: A ella le gusta, pero a mí no.
examples.en: She likes it, but I don't.
examples.note: The 'a + person' clarifies who — essential when the indirect object pronouns could be ambiguous.

sides.core: Encantar, molestar, doler, faltar, parecer — all follow the same reverse structure.

examples.note: Encantar = to love (things/activities). Same structure as gustar. Never 'amo el flamenco' for things — that's for people.

examples.en: I have a headache. (My head hurts me.)
examples.note: Doler follows gustar structure — the aching part is the subject. 'Tengo dolor de cabeza' also works.
The noise is what's doing the bothering — it's the subject. Molestar, like gustar, runs in reverse.

tricky: The most common error: 'yo gusto el café.' Wrong — gustar is never used this way. Also: 'me gustas' (I'm attracted to you / I like you as a person) vs 'me gusta' referring to a thing. And 'gustar' between people means romantic attraction — use 'caerle bien' for friendly liking: 'me cae bien' = I like him (as a person).

title: tomar
tagline: Tomar is 'to take' in its broadest sense — drink, eat, catch transport, make decisions. Common in Latin America; coger fills many of the same roles in Spain.

sides.core: Drinking, eating, and general taking — especially strong in Latin American Spanish.

examples.en: I have/drink coffee in the mornings.
examples.note: Tomar = to drink (especially in Latin America). In Spain 'tomar' also works but 'beber' is more common for drinking.

examples.en: What are you going to have?
examples.note: The universal waiter's question across Latin America. Equivalent of 'what can I get you?'
Tomar as an imperative — 'take this.' The single syllable 'toma' is very common in handoffs.

sides.core: Catching transport, taking routes, and taking decisions — all tomar territory.

examples.es: Tomo el metro para ir al trabajo.
examples.en: I take the metro to work.
examples.note: Transport: tomar el autobús, tomar el tren, tomar un taxi — all standard in Latin America and used in Spain too.

examples.en: A decision needs to be made.
examples.note: Tomar una decisión = to make a decision. Never 'hacer una decisión.'
Tomar algo en serio/a broma — to take something seriously/as a joke. Fixed phrases.

tricky: In Spain, 'coger el autobús' is standard; in Latin America, 'coger' has an obscene meaning so 'tomar' does that job instead. Knowing your audience matters. Also: 'tomarle el pelo a alguien' = to pull someone's leg — tomar doing idiom duty.

title: coger
tagline: In Spain: totally normal — grab, take, catch. In most of Latin America: an obscenity. The single most regionally dangerous verb in Spanish.

sides.core: Standard, everyday verb — grab, take, catch, pick up. Used constantly in Spain without any issue.

examples.es: Coge el autobús, es más rápido.
examples.note: Completely normal in Spain. In Mexico or Argentina, say 'toma el autobús' instead.
Physical grabbing or taking an object. Everyday Spanish in Spain.
Coger an illness = to catch it. Use 'agarrar un resfriado' in Latin America.

sides.core: Has an explicit sexual meaning across most of Latin America — use tomar, agarrar, or tomar instead.

examples.es: Agarra el libro que está en la mesa.
examples.en: Grab the book on the table.
examples.note: Agarrar = grab/take — safe everywhere. The replacement verb for coger in Latin America.

examples.es: Toma el primer desvío a la derecha.
examples.en: Take the first turn on the right.
examples.note: Tomar for directions and transport — the universal safe option.

examples.en: Can you pick this up off the floor?
examples.note: Recoger = to pick up, collect. Another safe alternative for the physical 'take/grab' meaning.

tricky: A Spanish person who moves to Mexico will get very funny looks the first week. The fix is simple: use 'agarrar' for grab, 'tomar' for take/catch, 'recoger' for pick up — and you're safe everywhere. 'Coger' is only truly safe in Spain and a few other places.

title: entrar
tagline: To enter — sounds simple, but the preposition after it (en vs a) divides Spain and Latin America, and it often replaces 'go in' in ways English doesn't.

sides.core: Moving into a space — and crucially, Spanish uses entrar where English might say 'go in.'

examples.es: Entra en casa. / Entra a la casa.
examples.note: 'Entrar en' is standard in Spain; 'entrar a' is standard in Latin America. Both are correct — know your audience.

examples.es: No me entra en la cabeza.
examples.en: I can't get my head around it.
examples.note: Figurative entrar — information not going in. Common idiom.
Entrar for clothes fitting — the item either goes in (fits) or doesn't. Very colloquial.

sides.core: Entrar generates idioms around things clicking, fitting, and coming over someone.

examples.note: Sueño or hunger entering you — the sensation coming over you. Vivid and very natural.

examples.en: I can't get into this topic / I can't grasp this.
examples.note: Subject matter not entering the brain — academic or intellectual struggle.
The panic entered him. This construction for emotions overtaking someone is very Spanish.

tricky: Entrar is intransitive — you don't 'entrar something,' you enter a place. The door enters nothing: 'entrar por la puerta' (enter through the door), not 'entrar la puerta.' And remember: en vs a is a genuine regional split, not a mistake on either side.

title: subir vs bajar
tagline: Up vs down — but also upload vs download, turn up vs turn down, get on vs get off. One axis, many contexts.

sides.core: Go up, rise, get on transport, upload, turn up volume or price.

examples.note: Volume, heat, brightness — subir for increasing intensity. Not 'aumenta la música.'
Digital upload = subir. The metaphor of sending something up to the cloud works perfectly.
Subir a = to get on/into transport. You go up into it.

sides.core: Go down, descend, get off transport, download, turn down volume or price.

examples.note: Reducing anything — volume, price, temperature. The opposite of subir.
Download = bajar. The data comes down to you. Very natural, very current.
Bajar de = get off/out of transport. You come down from it.

tricky: Subir and bajar both take direct objects for physical things you carry: 'sube las maletas' (take the bags up), 'baja la basura' (take the rubbish down). And prices: 'han subido los precios' (prices have gone up) — the prices are the subject. Never 'han aumentado los precios subir.'

title: tirar vs sacar
tagline: Tirar is throw/pull/bin. Sacar is take out/get/produce. Both get confused with each other and with other verbs.

sides.core: Throw, pull, knock over, throw away, or waste — a surprisingly violent range of meanings.

examples.en: Take the rubbish out / bin it.
examples.note: Throw it away — tirar is the verb for binning things. Nothing to do with taking the bin outside (that's sacar).
Tirar de = to pull. The opposite of empujar (push). Doors in Spain are often labelled tirar/empujar.

examples.en: He knocked the cup onto the floor.
examples.note: Threw or knocked — tirar for things ending up on the floor, deliberately or not.

sides.core: Take out, get something, produce, take a photo, or achieve a result.

examples.note: Take it out of the house to the bin. Compare: tirar la basura = throw it in the bin. Easy to mix up.
Photos are always sacar — you extract the image. Never 'toma una foto' in Spain (though common in Latin America).
Sacar = to get/achieve results. Very common for exams, competitions, outcomes.

tricky: 'Tirar la basura' (throw the rubbish in the bin) vs 'sacar la basura' (take the rubbish bag outside). Same rubbish, same English phrase 'take out the rubbish' — two different Spanish verbs depending on the action. Learners use them interchangeably and get corrected.

title: echar
tagline: Echar might be the most surprisingly versatile verb in Spanish — it means throw, pour, fire, miss someone, and powers a huge number of fixed expressions.

sides.core: Throw out, pour, add, or sack someone — the physical throwing/placing sense.

examples.note: Echar a alguien = to throw someone out, fire them. Very common. Not 'despedir' (which also works but is more formal).
Echar = to pour/add an ingredient. Very natural in cooking instructions.

examples.en: They showed the film last night.
examples.note: Echar una película = to show/screen a film. What's on TV: '¿qué echan esta noche?'

sides.core: Echar de menos, echar de ver, echarse a reír — echar powers some of the most important fixed expressions.

examples.note: Echar de menos = to miss someone or something. One of the most important phrases to know. 'Te extraño' is the Latin American equivalent.

examples.es: Se echó a reír / a llorar.
examples.note: Echarse a + infinitive = to suddenly start doing something. Always for sudden, involuntary action.
Echar una mano = to lend a hand. Echar un vistazo = to have a quick look. Echar la culpa = to blame. The expressions are endless.

tricky: 'Echar de menos' (to miss) vs 'extrañar' — in Spain you 'echo de menos' people; in Latin America you 'extraño' them. Using the wrong one doesn't cause confusion but reveals where you learned your Spanish. And 'echar' in expressions is almost always non-literal — don't try to unpack it logically.

title: caer
tagline: Caer is 'to fall' — but in Spanish it also expresses how you feel about people, whether things suit you, and moments of realisation.

sides.core: Physical falling and things dropping, figuratively and literally.

examples.note: Caerse (reflexive) for the fall itself. Caer is the base verb; caerse emphasises the whole event.
The phone fell from me — accidental drop uses this reflexive construction. Very natural.
Literary use of caer for time/light. Night, dusk, silence can all 'fall' in Spanish.

sides.core: How people land with you, things clicking, and idioms built around falling.

examples.en: I like / don't like him (as a person).
examples.note: Caer bien/mal = to make a good/bad impression. This is how you express friendly liking — not gustar. 'Me gusta' for people suggests attraction.

examples.en: I get it now. / Now I see.
examples.note: Caer for understanding — the penny dropping. '¡Ya caí!' is the moment of realisation.

examples.en: When is your birthday? (what day does it fall on?)
examples.note: Dates 'fall' in Spanish. '¿En qué día cae?' = what day does it fall on? Used for days of the week.

tricky: 'Me cae bien' (I like him as a person — he makes a good impression) vs 'me gusta' (I'm attracted to him / I like it). Using 'me gusta' for a person you platонically like can accidentally imply attraction. 'Me cae bien' is the safe, friendly option.

title: sentar vs sentarse
tagline: Sentarse is 'to sit down' — reflexive, which learners often drop. But sentar (without reflexive) means 'to suit' or 'to agree with' you physically.

sides.core: To sit down — always reflexive. The reflexive 'se' is not optional.

examples.note: Imperative of sentarse — the reflexive is built in. 'Sienta aquí' means something else entirely.
Third person plural — reflexive agrees. Never drop it.
The action of sitting — then waiting. Reflexive marks it as affecting you.

sides.core: To suit, to agree with physically, or to sit someone else down. Gustar-type structure for well-being.

examples.es: Ese color te sienta muy bien.
examples.note: Sentar bien = to suit/become. Works like gustar — the colour is the subject. Fashion and appearance.

examples.es: La comida picante no me sienta bien.
examples.en: Spicy food doesn't agree with me.
examples.note: Food agreeing or disagreeing with your stomach — sentar bien/mal. Very common.

examples.es: Le sentó mal lo que le dijiste.
examples.en: What you said didn't sit well with him.
examples.note: Emotional: something sitting badly — an offence or upset. Sentar mal for things that land badly.

tricky: 'Siéntate' (sit down — reflexive command) vs 'sienta' which sounds similar but comes from sentar and means 'it suits.' In practice the context makes it clear, but learners saying 'sienta aquí' when they mean 'sit here' cause momentary confusion.

title: seguir
tagline: Seguir means to follow AND to continue — and the structure 'seguir + gerund' is one of the most useful in Spanish.

sides.core: Physical following, following instructions, and following on social media.

examples.note: Physical direction — follow the person. Formal command.
Digital following. Seguir is the standard verb for social media follows.
Following rules, recipes, instructions — always seguir.

sides.core: Seguir + gerund = to keep doing, to still be doing. One of the most natural structures in Spanish.

examples.en: I'm still studying Spanish. / I keep studying Spanish.
examples.note: Seguir + gerund is elegant. 'Continúo estudiando' also works but seguir is more colloquial and warm.

examples.en: Are you still living in Madrid?
examples.note: Checking if a state continues. Very natural way to catch up with someone.

examples.es: Sigue recto y luego gira a la derecha.
examples.en: Go straight on and then turn right.
examples.note: Sigue (imperative) for directions — continue straight. Not 'continúa recto' which works but sounds stiff.

tricky: Seguir + gerund vs seguir + infinitive: 'sigo estudiando' (I keep studying — ongoing) vs the infinitive after seguir doesn't work. Also: 'seguir sin + infinitive' = to still not be doing: 'sigo sin entenderlo' = I still don't understand it. Extremely useful negative continuation.

title: esperar
tagline: Esperar covers both 'to wait' and 'to hope' — two very different things in English, handled by one verb in Spanish.

sides.core: Waiting for something or someone — physical, temporal.

examples.note: Direct command. Simple waiting.

examples.en: He'd been waiting for two hours.
examples.note: Duration of waiting — llevar + gerund of esperar. Very natural combination.
Esperar a que + subjunctive — waiting for an event to happen.

sides.core: Hoping for outcomes — triggers subjunctive when there's a second subject.

examples.note: Hope + subjunctive — the classic trigger. Espero que = I hope that + subjunctive, every time.
First person plural — let's hope. Subjunctive of esperar used as a mild collective wish.
Fixed phrase — entirely predictable. 'Era de esperar que pasara esto' = it was only to be expected.

tricky: Context usually separates waiting from hoping — you wait for a person or event, you hope for an outcome. But 'espero el resultado' could mean both (I'm waiting for the result / I'm hoping for the result). Spanish doesn't always force you to choose, which is poetic but occasionally ambiguous.

title: conseguir
tagline: Conseguir means to get, achieve, or manage to do something — not to 'follow' (that's confusing it with seguir). One of the most useful verbs learners underuse.

sides.core: Getting something through effort — obtaining, achieving, securing.

examples.note: Getting through effort or luck — conseguir for results and outcomes. Stronger than 'obtener' in everyday speech.
Sourcing or obtaining — where can it be found/bought. Natural everyday question.

examples.es: Consiguió una entrada para el concierto.
examples.en: He got a ticket for the concert.
examples.note: Getting something that required effort, luck, or persistence.

sides.core: Managing to do something — the 'manage to' structure that learners often miss.

examples.en: I can't manage to understand it.
examples.note: Conseguir + infinitive = to manage to do. Softer than poder — implies repeated effort, not just ability.

examples.en: I finally managed to get to sleep.
examples.note: After a struggle — conseguir marks that it took effort to achieve it.

examples.en: Did you manage to get in touch with them?
examples.note: The effort and achievement together in one verb. Learners say 'pude' but conseguí implies it wasn't easy.

tricky: Conseguir vs poder: 'puedo hacerlo' (I'm able to do it — capacity) vs 'consigo hacerlo' (I manage to do it — with effort). Conseguir implies the thing was difficult. Using it instead of poder makes your Spanish sound considerably more native.

title: crear vs creer
tagline: One letter apart, completely different meanings — crear is to create, creer is to believe. Constantly confused in writing and sometimes in speech.

sides.core: To create — making something that didn't exist before.

examples.note: Creation of something — the act of bringing it into existence.

examples.es: El artista crea desde la experiencia.
examples.note: Abstract creation — artistic production. No confusion with creer here.
Generating an outcome — sometimes crear = to cause, generate. Very natural.

sides.core: To believe, to think (opinion), or to believe in something — the cornerstone opinion verb.

examples.note: The most natural 'I think' for opinions. Enormously common.
Negated creer reliably triggers subjunctive. One of the clearest rules in Spanish.
Reflexive creerse = to believe something about yourself or to believe something at all. Very expressive.

tricky: The typo/slip of 'creo una empresa' (I believe a company??) instead of 'creo una empresa' — wait, those are spelled the same in present tense first person! The confusion hits hardest in other forms: 'creó' (he created) vs 'creyó' (he believed). The accent makes all the difference.
